The accessible labels of comparison-table\n    support marks now remain within their icons, and responsive feature and harness cards can shrink to the viewport\n    instead of creating an empty scrollable area at the right edge.\n\n-   Redesigned the **ptbk coder** landing page benefits around unattended PRD runs, portable `.book` agents, and PRD/code state that travels together in git commits. The visual cards now use centered code-native illustrations, and the comparison table brings those three advantages to the top.\n\n-   Fixed cyclic Agents Server `FROM` inheritance so resolution stops at the cycle edge as if it used `FROM @Null`.\n    Pages and APIs now continue to resolve while the existing Book editor warning identifies the cycle for repair.\n\n-   Fixed the Book editor `PERSONA` deprecation diagnostic regression test to assert the replacement guidance defined in the shared commitment catalog.\n\n-   Deprecated `PERSONA` for newly created Agents Server books. New-agent boilerplates and onboarding templates now use `GOAL` and `RULE` commitments, while the Book editor yellow-underlines every commitment marked as deprecated in the shared catalog and explains its replacement.\n\n-   Fixed the Agents Server's effective `FROM` inheritance handling. An explicitly selected parent now fully replaces\n    implicit Adam inheritance, while that parent's own chain is still materialized normally; only the final `FROM`\n    participates in both runtime resolution and missing-reference diagnostics. The Book editor now warns directly on\n    local inheritance cycles and when the core Adam agent does not explicitly inherit from `@Null`/`@Void`.\n\n-   Made **`@Adam` the implicit ancestor of every agent**, so a book that says nothing about inheritance behaves\n    exactly like one writing `FROM @Adam` or `FROM {Adam}`. An agent that should start from nothing says so explicitly\n    with `FROM @Null` (or `FROM {Void}`), and the Book language manual now documents both halves of that rule.\n\n    -   **A missing Adam stopped being silent.** Because the ancestor is implicit, a server whose core `Adam` agent had\n        been deleted inherited nothing without ever saying so. The Book editor now shows the very same \"referenced\n        agent was not found\" card on its right panel as if the book had written `FROM {Adam}` itself — right away,\n        without the author having to write the reference first to discover the problem. Whether a core agent is there\n        is read from the same status the Core Agents page renders, so the card and the page it links to can never\n        disagree, and a namesake on a federated server never hides an ancestor this server cannot actually load.\n    -   **The card offers the repair, not just the complaint.** A core agent is bundled with the server, so instead of\n        the ordinary \"create it from scratch\" button the card reinstates it from its repository book, names every other\n        core agent missing at the same time — one click brings back all of them — and links to the Core Agents admin\n        page. Reinstating is offered only to administrators, runs through the same reinstate flow the home page notice\n        and the Core Agents page already use, and refreshes the panel once the agents are back.\n    -   The same recovery is attached to an explicitly written reference, so `FROM {Adam}` on a server without Adam\n        offers to reinstate the core agent instead of creating an empty one that would shadow it.\n    -   **A book that declares its parent twice no longer breaks.** An agent has exactly one parent, so a repeated\n        `FROM` used to abort the whole resolution with an error. The last `FROM` now simply wins and overrides every\n        earlier one, which are dropped from the resolved source instead of being loaded, and the Book editor warns on\n        every `FROM` keyword involved — telling the overridden ones which line took their place.\n    -   Implicit inheritance recognizes the current agent's URL aliases as well as its canonical URL, preventing the\n        Adam core agent from resolving as its own parent when it is addressed by a name URL but stored under a\n        permanent-ID URL.\n    -   **A reinstated Adam is found again.** The implicit ancestor is addressed by the well-known name `adam`, and an\n        agent name used to resolve to the oldest agent that ever carried it — including one sitting in the recycle bin.\n        On a server where the core `Adam` had been deleted and reinstated, the name therefore pointed at the deleted\n        leftover, its source could no longer be loaded, and every book without `FROM` quietly inherited nothing while\n        an explicitly written `FROM @Adam` kept working, because that path resolves through the list of agents that\n        exist. An agent that exists now always wins over a deleted namesake, so both halves of the rule agree again. A\n        deleted agent stays resolvable when no live agent answers to that name, which is how the recycle bin restores\n        one.\n\n-   Added a **planned-message manager** to the Agents Server, so an administrator can finally see and steer every\n    timeout every agent planned — not only the one agent whose goal chat happens to be open. It lives in the same tab\n    group as the task manager, because the task manager answers \"what is running right now\" while this answers \"what\n    keeps making it run\".\n\n    -   **The whole life of a plan, in one place.** Planned messages are listed with the wake-ups still ahead, the ones\n        whose starting date has not arrived yet, the ones waking an agent right now, the ones being held back, and the\n        ones that are over — whether they were cancelled, ran out of runs, or passed their ending date. A finished plan\n        keeps its row and says which of those three ended it, so the manager also answers what a planned message did\n        before it stopped.\n    -   **Steering, not just watching.** Any planned message of any agent can be re-planned, held back and let go\n        again, or cancelled. Re-planning goes through the very same planned-message service an agent re-plans itself\n        with, so an administrator can never write a schedule the agent itself could not have written, and a planned\n        message that is firing at that very moment says so instead of quietly losing the change.\n    -   **Filters made of the plan itself.** The listing narrows by stage, by agent, by how often a message repeats\n        (a fixed interval, a cron, or a single wake-up), by when it last woke its agent, and by free text over the\n        message, its agent, its chat, and its owner. Every row links straight to the agent that planned it and to the\n        chat it wakes.\n\n-   Turned Agents Server planned messages from \"repeats every N milliseconds until cancelled\" into a real schedule, so\n    an agent can plan a message that repeats, one that runs exactly once, and anything between the two. Each planned\n    message can now carry a **cron expression**, a **total number of runs**, and a **starting and ending date**, and it\n    finishes by itself once that schedule is over.\n\n    -   **One schedule, one place deciding it.** A planned message follows either a fixed interval or a five-field cron\n        expression, bounded by `startsAt`, `endsAt`, and `maxRunCount`. A single resolver answers when the message wakes\n        the agent first, when it wakes it again, and when the plan is over, so scheduling, repeating, and finishing can\n        never disagree. The cron engine is the one already used by the automatic VPS self-update, which was extracted\n        into a shared utility instead of being written a second time.\n    -   **A finished plan disappears.** A message that ran as many times as it was planned to run, or whose ending date\n        passed, becomes terminal instead of being re-armed, and a wake-up delayed past its own ending date is dropped\n        rather than fired late. Finished messages are therefore never listed to the agent, never sent into its prompt,\n        and never wake it again — the agent only ever sees what is still ahead.\n    -   **The agent can re-plan, not only plan and cancel.** A new `update` action changes the schedule or the text of a\n        planned message while keeping its identifier, so a wake-up an agent already announced stays the same wake-up.\n        Only the named fields change, and `null` removes a bound.\n    -   **From every invocation.** Planning, re-planning, and cancelling work the same way from a normal chat, from an\n        external chat such as an email or API conversation, from a goal chat woken by a planned message itself, and from\n        the goal-chat turn queued when the agent's book was updated — all of them go through the one shared\n        planned-message service, reached through the planned-message sidecar of the answering runner, the model tools,\n        or the internal runtime API.\n    -   The goal chat lists the cron, the run counter, and the date window next to the repeat interval it showed before,\n        and the wake-up message itself now says which run of the plan it is.\n\n-   Made every Agents Server agent project a git repository whose history is written by the agent itself, and turned\n    the popup behind a **📁 project** chip into a card that is actually worth opening. Clicking the chip used to show\n    little more than the project directory name; it now shows what the project is, what state it is in, and the exact\n    diff of what that very message did to it.\n\n    -   **Every project is a git repository.** The local agent runner initializes one for a project which is not a\n        repository yet and commits everything an answer changed into it, under the same message as the answered\n        message itself. Agents are told about this in their projects prompt section, so nothing has to `git init` or\n        commit by hand anymore, and work done in a project stays recoverable and reviewable as normal history. A\n        project which already belongs to a repository around the agent folder is deliberately left to that\n        repository instead of being turned into an embedded one, and a freshly initialized repository gets ignore\n        rules so installed dependencies and `.env` secrets never enter an automatic commit.\n    -   **The card shows the project.** Its running state and status label, a link opening the running project in a\n        new tab, a link opening its project page in a new tab, plus its size, file count and whether it is a git\n        repository — all resolved through the same helpers the project page itself uses, so the chip and the page it\n        links to can never describe one project differently.\n    -   **The card shows the change.** How many files the message changed with the added and removed line counts, the\n        commit it created, the list of changed files, and the unified diff itself with added, removed and context\n        lines told apart. A change too large to carry into a chat is shortened and says so.\n    -   A project the answer committed something into now gets a chip even when nothing in the harness log named it,\n        because a project that was changed was obviously worked with.\n\n-   Added Agents Server chips below a chat answer for every source outside the agent it touched, so an answer never\n    silently reaches beyond the agent again. An agent that reviews a Gmail mailbox and drafts a mail now says so with\n    a **🔌 Gmail** chip below its message, exactly like the project and wake-up chips already added next to the source\n    chips that show the knowledge behind an answer.\n\n    This completes the same universal pattern rather than adding a second one: the local agent runner resolves what\n    the answering coding harness really reached from its live runtime log — which is deleted the moment a message is\n    answered — reports it in the run-report sidecar it already writes, and the server turns each source into one chip\n    on the assistant message. The chips therefore show up in normal chats, in the goal chat, and when an external\n    chat such as an email conversation is opened, while the outbound email itself is still rendered from the answer\n    text alone and stays unchanged.\n\n    -   **Integrations** such as Gmail or Google Calendar are recognized from the integration tool calls of both\n        supported harnesses and shown under their human-readable name.\n    -   **Websites** are shown by hostname, both when the harness fetched an address directly and when it ran a\n        network client such as `curl` or `wget` in the shell.\n    -   **Web searches** are shown with the query that was looked up.\n    -   Work an agent does only inside itself still produces no chip at all. Only harness tool payloads are\n        inspected, so an address or service merely mentioned in the conversation — or written into a file the agent\n        edits — is never reported as touched, and addresses of the machine the agent runs on are dropped because they\n        are internal.\n\n-   Added `--period <duration>` to `ptbk coder ping`. Without it the ping stays exactly what it was — one tiny dummy\n    prompt, one reported result, done. With it that very same ping repeats once per period until it is stopped with\n    `CTRL+C`, which keeps the quota window of a harness permanently refreshing for a handful of tokens per ping.\n    Pinging `claude-code` with `--period 5h` therefore keeps the **Claude Code 5-hour limit window always open**, so a\n    queue started at any hour already has a fresh window waiting instead of burning the first minutes of it.\n\n    -   The period is measured from the start of one ping to the start of the next one, so `--period 5h` really pings\n        every 5 hours instead of every 5 hours plus however long a ping happens to take. It is a wall-clock deadline,\n        so a computer which falls asleep during a period does not stretch it.\n    -   A ping which fails is reported and the loop simply continues with the next period, because a keep-alive which\n        dies on the first hiccup is not a keep-alive.\n    -   The duration uses the same `5h`, `30m`, `1h30m` format as the `--wait-*` options of `ptbk coder run` and is\n        rejected when it is not a positive one, so `--period` can never become a loop without a pause between rounds.\n    -   The `ptbk coder` landing page presents this as an advanced feature of its own.\n\n-   Fixed Agents Server planned-message chips hiding the numeric part of their scheduled time. The chip now uses the\n    shared chat typography for its text while retaining the existing OpenMoji fallback for its stopwatch icon, so a\n    label such as **“Timeout: 10:28 AM”** renders exactly as it is copied.\n\n-   Fixed misleading **Goal Chat** response timing. The old label measured from the time a message entered the local\n    runner queue, so a scheduled wake-up could claim it took many hours to answer even when the agent had only just\n    run. The coding harness now records its real start and finish times in the existing answer report; the server uses\n    those timestamps for the completed answer's time and duration. Goal Chat now says **“executed for …”**, while an\n    older runner report with no execution timing shows no misleading queue-age duration.\n\n-   Changed Agents Server goal-chat planned messages from `setTimeout` to `setInterval`. A planned message used to be\n    consumed by its own firing, so an agent whose goal is \"check emails every 5 minutes\" had to re-plan the very same\n    wake-up on every single invocation — and the moment one answer forgot to, the goal chat was left with **No planned\n    messages** and the agent never woke up again.\n\n    A planned message now repeats at the interval it was planned with until it is cancelled, which makes **keeping the\n    current plan the default**: an invoked agent sees its planned messages with their intervals and does nothing at all\n    while they still match its goal. When the goal changes to \"every 10 minutes\", the agent cancels the message that no\n    longer matches and sets one with the interval its goal now requires.\n\n    -   The durable timeout of a repeating message is re-armed in place after each firing instead of scheduling a\n        successor row, so one plan keeps one `timeoutId` for its whole life. The identifier an agent saw while it was\n        answering therefore still cancels the message when its answer is applied minutes later, and a crash between two\n        repetitions can never leave two schedules behind.\n    -   The wake-up turn of each repetition stays idempotent by carrying how many times its timeout already fired.\n    -   The planned-message sidecar, the runtime tools, the goal-chat notes, and the planned-message panel of the goal\n        chat all show the repeat interval, so an agent (and a person) can compare the plan with the goal instead of\n        guessing from a single due time.\n    -   An interval shorter than one minute is rejected, because a repeating message with a tiny interval would be an\n        unattended self-invocation loop rather than a plan.\n\n-   Fixed an Agents Server agent referencing a project it just created as a plain link, which turned into a proper\n    project chip only after the page was reloaded. Every mention of a project — its `[[project-name]]` token, its\n    display name in prose, a link to its project page, or its public project URL — becomes a chip by matching the\n    message against the project references the chat holds, and those references were resolved once while the server\n    rendered the page. A project created during the conversation simply did not exist yet at that moment.\n\n    The open chat now reloads its project references whenever the agent finishes an answer, so the chip appears with\n    the answer that announces the project instead of after a reload. Answers still being generated are ignored — their\n    content keeps changing while the progress card updates, which says nothing about the projects on the server — and\n    the answers already rendered when the chat opens arrive together with their projects, so opening a chat reloads\n    nothing. Building the references walks every project folder, therefore the server first compares the project\n    directory names against the ones the chat already renders and rebuilds them only when the set really changed.\n\n    The chips themselves are unchanged: one shared hook still feeds the chat, the profile preview, and the private-mode\n    chat, and the permission deciding whether a chat may see projects at all now lives in a single resolver shared by\n    the agent page, the chat page, and the reload.\n\n-   Added Agents Server chips below a chat answer for the projects it worked with and the wake-ups it planned,\n    next to the source chips that already show the knowledge behind an answer.\n\n    -   **Projects:** the local agent runner resolves which `projects/<project-name>/` folders the answering coding\n        harness really used — viewed or edited — from its live runtime log, which is deleted the moment a message is\n        answered. The projects are reported in the run-report sidecar the runner already writes next to the answered\n        message, and the server turns each of them into one chip showing the same human-readable project name and\n        link as every other project surface. Only harness tool payloads are inspected and every project is matched\n        against the projects that really exist, so a project merely mentioned in the conversation, or a\n        `projects/<project-name>/` placeholder from the prompt, never produces a chip.\n    -   **Planned messages:** applying the planned-message sidecar now returns what was really scheduled or\n        cancelled, and each applied command becomes one timeout chip. This revives the timeout chip and its detail\n        popup that `<Chat/>` already implements for `set_timeout` / `cancel_timeout`, instead of leaving the planned\n        wake-up visible only as raw text such as `timeoutId: tmo_…` inside the answer.\n\n    Both chips ride the assistant message as tool calls, so they show up in normal chats, in the goal chat, and when\n    an external chat such as an email conversation is opened in the Agents Server — while the outbound email itself\n    is rendered from the answer text alone and stays unchanged.\n\n-   Fixed a flaky `$spawnLoggedBashScript` coder test that could fail `npm run test-for-ptbk-coder` before any\n    coding prompt started. Waiting for the test harness fixture to boot reused the process-tree termination budget,\n    even though booting it pays for a full Bash login shell whose cost belongs to the machine - profiles loading a\n    version manager need about ten seconds on Windows, and parallel Jest workers multiply that. Fixture startup now\n    has its own budget, and a wrapper shell that exits before the harness starts fails immediately with its exit\n    code, signal, and captured output instead of timing out silently.\n\n-   Fixed Agents Server agents announcing a planned goal-chat message that was never actually planned. Chat answers\n    are produced by a coding-agent runner in a separate process, and the only planning channel that runner had was a\n    documented `curl` snippet against `/api/internal/agent-goal-chat-planned-messages` — an optional shell command\n    with no verifiable artifact, so a model could (and did) write \"I also scheduled a follow-up check in one hour\"\n    while the goal chat kept showing **No planned messages** and no `⏳` note was ever recorded.\n\n    Planning is now a deterministic part of the runner contract, mirroring the proven TEAM-transcript sidecar\n    pattern instead of a network call:\n\n    -   Before a message is queued into the agent folder, the server writes `messages/planned/<message>.json` with\n        the agent's `currentPlannedMessages` (which also replaces `list_timeouts` — the harness simply sees them)\n        and an empty `commands` array.\n    -   The prompt section now teaches that editing this file is the **only** way to plan or cancel a wake-up,\n        that announcing one in the answer schedules nothing, and it explicitly allows changing the `commands` array\n        next to the existing `projects/` and TEAM-transcript allowances (the `## Projects` \"do not touch anything\n        outside\" line now defers to that single list instead of contradicting it).\n    -   When the finished answer is synchronized, the server applies every `{\"action\":\"set\",...}` /\n        `{\"action\":\"cancel\",...}` command through the very same `AGENT_GOAL_CHAT_PLANNED_MESSAGE_ACTIONS` service\n        that backs the model tools and the internal API, then deletes the sidecar so a repeated worker tick can\n        never plan the same wake-up twice. One rejected command is logged and never blocks the others or the\n        already answered message, and the sidecar is also dropped on cancellation, failure, and timeout.\n    -   The goal-chat lifecycle notes no longer instruct the agent to \"use `set_timeout`\" (a tool that does not\n        exist in a coding-runner invocation) but to really plan a wake-up, since announcing one changes nothing.\n\n    Kept from the previous fix: runner folder names normalize permanent ids to lowercase while goal-chat records use\n    their canonical IDs, so the internal scheduler resolves the canonical agent before setting, listing, or\n    cancelling a planned message.\n\n-   Fixed unknown uppercase Book commitments in the Agents Server. They now terminate the preceding commitment,\n    remain visible as red-underlined editor errors, and are appended only as final extra context in the generated\n    system message rather than leaking into the preceding commitment's behavior or prompt suffix.\n\n-   Added an Agents Server administration email testing tool. Administrators can compose and send mail through the\n    bundled Stalwart service, use existing agent addresses to pre-fill sender and recipient fields, and inspect the\n    persisted result in Messages. Normal administrators are restricted to sender addresses on their current server;\n    the VPS superadmin can test any sender domain.\n\n-   Fixed Windows executable discovery to check the system `PATH` before the conventional installation directories, so\n    LibreOffice installed through a package manager's command shim can be located for legacy-document processing.\n    The LibreOffice locator now has deterministic configuration coverage, while the shared Windows locator has\n    filesystem-backed coverage for `PATH` discovery.\n\n-   Fixed `ptbk coder run --test-before yes-and-fix` failing at the first prompt when its pre-coding verification\n    generated repository changes. Promptbook now snapshots the tree before that test and commits exactly the files it\n    changed before continuing to a queued or repair prompt, pushes that commit when `--auto-push` is enabled, and does\n    not create an empty commit when the test changed nothing.\n\n-   Fixed `ptbk coder` leaving a coding harness running after the coder process stops. Every temporary runner shell now\n    owns its full harness process tree and watches its parent coder process, so a normal exit, termination signal,\n    crash, or fatal out-of-memory exit terminates all nested harness processes on Windows, macOS, and Linux.\n\n-   Fixed macOS portability of the Promptbook CLI installation detection tests by resolving temporary project paths before comparing them with `process.cwd()`.\n\n-   Added automatic Promptbook CLI update checks when `ptbk coder run` starts in an interactive terminal, both for the default automatic queue and for `--no-auto` per-prompt confirmation. Before starting the coding queue, Promptbook now finds directly declared local `ptbk` / `@promptbook/cli` dependencies and directly installed global CLI packages, compares every installation with npm, and offers one confirmation when any of them is outdated. An approved update preserves each local package's existing `dependencies` or `devDependencies` placement, updates global installations globally, handles local and global installations together, and then asks for a fresh invocation so the running process cannot continue with already-loaded old code or a newly changed project manifest. Non-TTY runs do not perform the check. The npm registry lookup, version parsing, install-command construction, and TTY approval prompt are shared with the existing coding-harness updater; Promptbook's numbered prerelease revisions are compared semantically, so versions such as `0.114.0-8` and `0.114.0-9` no longer collapse into the same release.\n\n-   Fixed Agents Server chat project chips. Their popup menu is no longer clipped by the general markdown-details\n    styling, so clicking a chip reliably reveals its running-state indicator plus the **Open the project in a new tab**\n    and **Open the project page in a new tab** actions. Existing and older chat messages now recognize an agent\n    project by its display name as well as its `[[technical-name]]` token, project-page/file link, or public URL, while\n    preserving unrelated links. Project chips now show the project's favicon with the same initials fallback as other\n    project surfaces, display an explicit red or green runtime indicator, and expose a direct **Start the project** or\n    **Stop the project** action. Opening a stopped project remains available: the chip starts its runtime first and then\n    transfers the already-opened new tab to the project's public URL.\n\n-   Fixed the scrolling of the live terminal on the `ptbk coder` landing page, which **scrolled sideways and cut the agent visual off**. The terminal drew its dashboard at a fixed 96 columns in a fixed text size, no matter how much room the hero column really gave it, and the 214-character sample command was drawn on one endless row, so the session had to be scrolled horizontally to be read at all. On top of that, the box drawing characters of the dashboard frame, the shade of the progress bar and the status marks are missing from the latin subset of the terminal font, so the browser drew them from a fallback font in which they are up to 1.6 times wider than one character cell — that alone pushed the right border of every box out of the frame, which is why the boxes looked ragged even where the text fitted. Finally the body had a fixed height shorter than the whole sample and auto-scrolled to the latest line, so the agent visual was scrolled out of view exactly when the run was finished. The terminal now fits itself into the width it gets, the same way a terminal emulator fits its character grid into its window: it takes as many character cells as fit at the preferred text size, clamped to the same **56–96 columns** the real `ptbk coder run` frame is clamped to, and scales the text down when even 56 columns would not fit. The whole dashboard is rebuilt for that column count, so a phone gets the same 56-column dashboard the real CLI draws in a narrow terminal, and the typed command wraps onto the next rows like real terminal output instead of widening the terminal. Every character which the terminal font does not provide is measured in the browser and pulled back onto the character grid with letter spacing, so each row is exactly as wide as the cells it is counted as and the box borders line up again; the highlighted `DONE` badge and the control keys carry their padding as spaces of the sample itself for the same reason. The body is now as tall as the whole scripted session, so nothing scrolls in either direction and **the octopus agent visual stays fully visible** once the sample run has finished. Specified in [`apps/coder-landing/specs/components/live-terminal.md`](apps/coder-landing/specs/components/live-terminal.md).\n\n-   Fixed the `ptbk coder` landing page live terminal so its agent visual now uses the exact same shared animated\n    ANSI ASCII renderer as `ptbk coder run`, rather than showing the browser canvas avatar. The visual keeps the\n    developer agent book as its source and maps only the shared renderer's terminal colors to browser text spans.\n\n-   Fixed long-running rich `ptbk coder` sessions making VS Code lag after a terminal regains focus. Terminal frame\n    updates now batch all cursor movement and changed animated-avatar rows into one stdout write, instead of issuing a\n    write for every row, so the dashboard remains animated without building a large terminal-rendering backlog.\n\n-   Fixed goal-chat notices and planned-message panels covering the beginning of the conversation. The shared chat header\n    slot now reserves space above the messages instead of overlaying them.\n\n-   Made the Agents Server goal chat active rather than informational. Creating or changing an agent whose Book contains\n    a `GOAL` / `GOALS` commitment now queues a real turn in that agent's singleton goal chat, and the lifecycle message\n    includes the effective new goal. Every server chat invocation can now set, list, and cancel durable planned messages;\n    they are always stored for and fired into the singleton goal chat, where firing wakes the agent to act and optionally\n    plan its next invocation. The in-process AgentKit runtime and the managed coding-agent runner share the same\n    goal-chat scheduling operations, and the planned-message panel refreshes while a turn is running so new execution\n    times and cancellations appear without reopening the chat.\n\n-   Debounced the Agents Server’s automatic **“My book was updated”** goal-chat note independently for each agent. Book persistence retains its existing 1-second editor debounce, while the note is now written once, one minute after the latest successful source update, so typing no longer floods an agent’s goal chat.\n\n-   Fixed `ptbk coder generate-boilerplates --count N*M` so all `M` prompts in a generated file share one fresh emoji tag, while every generated file receives a different tag. Updated the `ptbk coder` landing page accordingly.\n\n-   Improved the one-line live progress in Agents Server local chats so it now follows the intended handoff from generic thinking to real work. The browser continues rotating the configured `THINKING_MESSAGES` while Codex has only private reasoning or an unknown command, rather than replacing it with the uninformative **“Considering the request.”** / **“Running a task.”** status. Once the runner emits a concrete activity, the existing progress card shows only that latest safe action — for example **“Inspecting relevant files.”**, **“Updating relevant files.”**, or **“Running tests.”** — and it does not regress to generic reasoning between actions. The shared resolver now recognizes equivalent PowerShell and Unix inspection/update commands, while still withholding raw reasoning, commands, arguments, paths, and tool payloads.\n\n-   Completed the Agents Server superadmin external-chat view: it now exposes the frozen chats of other users with a direct owner-profile link and an owner-filtered link to the recorded chat-history thread.\n\n-   Refactored multiline prompts, Book-language fixtures, SQL, CSS, generated text, and user-facing import/recovery messages across the repository to use `spaceTrim`. Nested runtime content now uses `block(...)` where it can span lines, while protocol delimiters and other boundary-sensitive strings remain explicit so their exact wire format is preserved.\n\n-   Made the Agents Server local coding-harness path honor the `TEAM` commitment without multiplying harness runs. A queued user turn now snapshots its resolved local teammates and their instructions into a per-message workspace, gives that roster to the one primary harness run, and retains any harness-created teammate `.book` transcripts alongside the finished message. The server parses those transcripts into ordinary `TEAM` tool calls, so the primary answer gets the existing teammate chip and mocked-chat modal, while each consulted local teammate receives a frozen `TEAM_MEMBER` external chat linked back to the invoking primary-agent thread. The existing Social Media Manager / Copywriter default-agent pair remains the runnable example of a compact `{Copywriter}` teammate reference.\n\n-   Fixed outbound Stalwart email delivery and improved the Agents Server `/admin/messages` dashboard:\n\n    -   Existing standalone VPS processes can retain the old bundled Stalwart endpoint `127.0.0.1:587` even after the installer writes the corrected `465` / implicit-TLS settings. The Stalwart provider now recognizes only that legacy local configuration and uses the real `submissions` listener on `465`; explicitly configured remote SMTP endpoints remain unchanged.\n    -   Inbound messages now show **Received** as soon as their durable `Message` row exists instead of being misclassified as **Pending** merely because received messages never have outbound send attempts.\n    -   Failed outbound rows now show the provider error immediately and expose every failed attempt in an expandable complete log with its id, timestamp, provider, result, readable stack trace, and untouched raw provider response.\n    -   Sender and recipient JSON is now rendered as compact **From** / **To** contact cards with separate display names and clickable, wrapping email addresses.\n\n-   Fixed the **self-contained Stalwart email server** of the Agents Server, which received mail but processed none of it: every inbound message landed in `/admin/messages` with an empty sender, an empty recipient list, no subject and a body that was the raw header block of the original message, and no agent chat was ever created from it. Three independent defects were behind that, each verified against the running mail server on `live.ptbk.io` and each reproduced byte for byte before it was changed. First, the DATA-stage MTA hook payload was reassembled into an RFC 5322 message with `` `${name}: ${value}` `` joined by CRLF, but Stalwart reports every header exactly as it stood on the wire — the value already carries the space after the colon and its own terminating line break, and folded values keep their inner line breaks. The reconstruction therefore wrote `Name:` followed by two spaces and, because the joined terminator was duplicated, an empty line after every header; that empty line closes the header block after the very first header, so `From`, `To`, `Subject` and `Message-ID` were parsed as message body and the transport values were lost. Header lines are now rebuilt from the raw value, and a payload carrying no header at all is refused with a branded `ParseError` instead of yielding a headerless message. Second, the hook route derived the mail domain and the worker origin from `request.nextUrl`, which behind the VPS reverse proxy describes the internal listener and resolves to `localhost` — so every recipient was filtered out as foreign, no agent was ever matched, and not even the unknown-agent answer was sent. Both values now come from the server registry through `$provideServer()`, the same single source of truth that already decides which server database the request writes to, so the mail domain, the database namespace and the worker wake-up can no longer disagree on a VPS hosting several servers. Third, once a chat was finally created its job was cancelled immediately with `Chat was deleted before it could be queued`, because the background runners load the chat through the viewer-facing `getUserChat`, which discloses the externally created sources (`EMAIL`, `OPENAI_API`, `TEAM_MEMBER`) to administrators only. The runners are not viewers — they own an already-persisted job and run under its owner's identity — so all three of them (`runUserChatJob`, `runImmediateUserChatAnswer` and the local agent runner) now share one `getUserChatForJobRunner` helper that states this once. No installer or mail-server configuration had to change: the bundled Stalwart was already provisioned correctly by `install.sh`, all three defects were on the Agents Server side.\n\n-   Added a **comparison section** to the `ptbk coder` landing page, which answers the one question a visitor who already codes with an agent has left: why not just run Claude Code, OpenAI Codex or opencode directly? The new `#comparison` section, the last one before the footer, compares `ptbk coder` with exactly those three in a table of fifteen capabilities — a whole backlog in one run, harness-agnostic runs, several agents on one backlog, tests before and after every task, commits under a separate agent identity, pull and push around each task, one worktree per task, the kanban board, the task state kept in git, the pacing for quota windows, the preflight ping, the generated backlog and the human in the loop. Every row is deliberately about the **orchestration around a task** and never about how well an agent writes code, every cell carries one of three marks — built in, reachable but you script it yourself, or not provided — together with the option, command or workaround behind it, and the two rows which `ptbk coder` does not win (the interactive coding session and the human in the loop) are kept in on purpose: the compared solutions are the very harnesses `ptbk coder` drives, so the table can only show what one layer adds above the other. The three compared columns take their display name, vendor and logo straight from the harness catalog of the page instead of repeating them, the marks of the cells and of the legend are one component, and the long-form explanation of each capability stays in the features section, which the footnote of the table links to. The capability column stays sticky while the table scrolls horizontally, so on a phone the first solution column is fully readable next to it. Specified in [`apps/coder-landing/specs/sections/comparison.md`](apps/coder-landing/specs/sections/comparison.md) and [`apps/coder-landing/specs/content/comparison-matrix.md`](apps/coder-landing/specs/content/comparison-matrix.md), and reachable from the header navigation as **Comparison**.\n\n-   Optimized `npm run test-app-agents-server` and every other Agents Server production build, without changing what is built, linted or tested. A single test run spent most of its time on work which was either repeated or needlessly serial. **`npx kill-port` is gone.** It was called twice per test run — once by `pretest-e2e` and once by `prebuild` — for a package which is not a declared dependency, so npm resolved it through the registry every single time; measured at 38 s on a cold npx cache and 7 s on a warm one. The new [`apps/agents-server/scripts/kill-port.js`](apps/agents-server/scripts/kill-port.js) frees the same ports through `netstat` on Windows and `lsof` elsewhere in under 0.2 s, refuses to stop the process which called it or its parent, and needs no network at all. **App linting no longer blocks the production build.** It reads only the sources, so `npm run test-e2e` now starts it next to the build and prints its output as one block once the build is over, which means a run waits for the slower of the two instead of for their sum — the lint alone took 79 s. Its result is also cached between runs now. **The homepage prerender is skipped for E2E builds.** Every build used to start one more production server just to download `/` into `.next/prerendered/home.html`, a snapshot which nothing in the repository ever reads; the new `--no-homepage-prerender` build argument is applied by every E2E build, because Playwright starts that very same build seconds later and the tests open the homepage for real. Normal production builds keep the prerender. **`generate-reserved-paths` stopped invalidating the caches of every build.** It ran through a type-checking `ts-node` (3.4 s instead of the 1.1 s of `--transpile-only`, while the app sources are type-checked by the build itself anyway) and it rewrote its generated file even when the reserved paths had not changed, which moved the modification time of a file imported by the middleware forward and invalidated the webpack and TypeScript caches of every build and every `npm run dev`; an unchanged file is now left untouched. Finally, **Next.js build workers are asked for explicitly.** Next.js turns them off as soon as a `webpack` function is configured — and with them it turns off the parallel output file tracing — so collecting the traces ran completely alone for 120 s of a 790 s build, between the compilation and the static generation. It now runs next to the remaining compilation and page generation, and compiling each target in its own short-lived worker process also releases the memory of that target as soon as it is done, which is the reason why the heap limit of the build moved from the command line of the build process into `NODE_OPTIONS`: a worker can inherit it only from there. A build which asks for a single build worker, as standalone VPS self-updates do, keeps the tracing serial, because such a build has to save memory rather than time — it still gains the per-target worker processes, which is exactly what its earlier out-of-memory kills came from. Measured back to back on one machine with a warm build cache, `npm run build-e2e -- --no-lint` went from 847 s to 334 s and the whole `npm run test-app-agents-server` finished in 759 s, running the same 19 tests with the same result as before.\n\n-   Agents Server projects are now shown with **their real title and their own icon**. A project card used to show the raw folder name — `prague-murders-map` cut to `prague-murde...` — next to the same generic folder glyph as every other project, so a board full of projects told the visitor nothing. The title is now resolved from the README heading, then from the `<title>` of the project `index.html`, and only then from the folder name, which is humanized as the last resort, so `prague-murders-map` reads as **Prague Murders Map** and the folder name stays below the title as the technical identifier. The icon is the favicon of the project — the icon linked by its `index.html`, or a favicon found in one of the conventional locations such as `favicon.ico` or `public/favicon.svg` — and a project without one gets an icon made of the initials of its name, `PMM` for `prague-murders-map`. Only an icon which really exists as an image file inside the project folder is used, an icon hosted elsewhere or a path escaping the project folder is refused, and the initials are shown whenever the favicon cannot be loaded — for example for a visitor who is not signed in and therefore may not read project files at all. Everything is resolved in one place, so the agent Projects dashboard, the admin all-projects dashboard, the project page and the compact project references show exactly the same title and the same icon, and the project domains table names every project by that same title; the chat project chip no longer humanizes the project name on its own, and the static project server and the project presentation now share one definition of what the `index.html` of a project is.\n\n-   `npm run test-unit` no longer **fails on Windows after every single test has already passed**. Jest gives each of its workers 500 ms to shut down and then force-kills it, and a worker of this repository regularly needs longer than that, so the force kill runs on practically every run. When it landed on a worker which was already terminating, Windows refused it with `EPERM`; Node reports such a refusal by emitting an `error` event on the child process, nobody listens for it, so the emit threw out of a bare timer callback and killed the whole run with exit code `1` — after a green `665 passed` summary. The run is now started through the guard which the Agents Server production build already used against the very same race, which moved to `scripts/ignore-kill-eperm.js` so that both callers share one copy, and which turns the refusal back into the `false` return value that `kill` documents. This only stops the run from dying on a cleanup race — the worker still exits too slowly, so the `A worker process has failed to exit gracefully` warning stays until the leaking handle behind it is found.\n\n-   Every commit created by `ptbk coder` now contains **only the files of the operation which created it**. Each committing command used to run a plain `git add .` first, so `ptbk coder add --commit` committed the new prompt file together with whatever else happened to be changed in the project, `ptbk coder verify --commit` committed the archived prompt file together with the work in progress of the developer sitting next to it, and a `ptbk coder run` round committed the prompt file, the files the coding agent changed, and every unrelated change which was in the working tree — the last one was only masked by the clean working tree check, which `--ignore-git-changes` turns off. Now each command captures the state of the working tree before it changes anything and commits exactly the files which really changed in between: the created prompt file for `add`, the generated prompt files for `generate-boilerplates`, the created and updated configuration files for `init`, the archived or repaired prompt file for `verify`, and the prompt file together with the files the coding agent changed for `run`, `server` and `--isolate`. Anything which was already changed before the command started is left in the working tree, including a file which was staged by hand. There is one shared mechanism behind all of it — one commit scope captured before the operation and resolved against the working tree afterwards — which the round commit also reuses to normalize the line endings of exactly those files, and `commitChanges` now takes one single list of the relevant paths instead of the two overlapping path options it had before. Because the relevant paths are derived from git itself, a file ignored through `.gitignore` (such as the `.env` which `ptbk coder init` writes) can never end up among them, so scoping the commit cannot break on an ignored path.\n\n-   United the DNS configuration manuals of the Agents Server. The DNS records of one server used to be spread over three different manuals with three different visuals: the generated project domains had their own indigo panel on `/superadmin/servers` without any Cloudflare wizard, the server domain got a separate amber panel right below it and only when its DNS was already broken, and the email records lived in a third manual on `/admin/email-server`. An administrator setting up a fresh server therefore had to walk three pages and paste the Cloudflare API token more than once. Now `/superadmin/servers` shows one manual per server which lists **everything the server needs at its DNS provider** — its own domain, the generated project domains, and its email — and configures all of it with one Cloudflare API token in one click. The manual is shown for every server, not only for a broken one, so the setup can also be reviewed and re-applied at any time. There is exactly one DNS component left, `<DnsRecordsInstructions/>`, which renders a list of DNS sections; a subpage passes only the sections which belong to it, so `/admin/email-server` keeps its email records in the same component and the same wizard and points to the Servers page for the complete setup. Each section may offer alternative setups — the generated project domains still offer the wildcard or single-project and the CNAME or A record variants — and the selected variant of every section feeds the one shared Cloudflare wizard. The wizard, its zone-file export and the `/api/admin/dns-records/cloudflare` endpoint now work with record groups instead of one flat record list, so a manual mixing required records (email) with alternatives (server and project domains) still writes exactly the recommended record of each alternative and never both sides of a conflict; duplicate records shared by two sections are written only once. DKIM records intentionally stay on `/admin/email-server`, because their public keys are generated by Stalwart and must not be invented.\n\n-   **Breaking:** Replaced the `--reverse` flag of `ptbk coder verify` with `--order <from-earliest|from-latest|random>`. The old flag only toggled between the two possible directions, which left no room for a third one; the new option names the order explicitly, so `ptbk coder verify --reverse` becomes `ptbk coder verify --order from-latest`. `from-earliest` stays the default and walks the prompt files from the oldest one, `from-latest` walks them from the newest one, and the new `random` shuffles the queue, which is useful when a long verification session keeps stopping on the same prompt files. Because the prompt files are reloaded after every single verification, `random` really reshuffles on each pass instead of picking one order for the whole run. The supported orders, their descriptions and their validation live in one shared definition used by the CLI command, its `--help` output and the standalone verification script, so the CLI refuses an unknown order with the list of the supported ones and the script refuses it with a branded error. The local VS Code coder terminal and the `ptbk coder` landing page were updated to the new option.\n\n-   Added an in-progress signal to `ptbk coder`. A prompt used to jump straight from not started `[ ]` to fully implemented `[x]`, so a queue running for hours never showed which task was being worked on and a coder which was killed or crashed left no trace of the interrupted task at all. Now the prompt file itself carries the intermediate `[^]` status, which is rewritten before every single step of the round, so it always names the harness, the model, the thinking level, the steps which already finished with their price and duration, and the step which is running right now — for example `` [^] by OpenAI Codex `gpt-5.6-luna` thinking `max` - Implementation in progress ``, then `` [^] by OpenAI Codex `gpt-5.6-luna` thinking `max` (ChatGPT account) - Implementation ~$0.2036 10 minutes; Testing in progress ``, and finally the unchanged `` [x] by OpenAI Codex `gpt-5.6-luna` thinking `max` (ChatGPT account) - Implementation ~$0.2036 10 minutes; Testing 35 minutes ``. Only the verified `[x]` state is committed, because the round commit is still created after the prompt has been implemented and verified. The `[^]` status is deliberately never reverted: a killed process, an internal error or any other interruption leaves it in the prompt file as the signal that this task was left in the middle, and such a prompt is not picked up again automatically. The in-progress and the done status lines are built from one shared formatter, so they can never drift apart; the `ptbk coder server` board shows a left-behind `[^]` prompt in its **In progress** column with a `[^]` tag, and `ptbk coder verify` no longer offers a file containing an interrupted prompt for archiving. Because the harness reports its authentication method only when a step finishes, the `(ChatGPT account)` part appears as soon as the first coding step is done. The `ptbk coder` landing page documents the new status.\n\n-   Added a running indicator to the Agents Server **System** menu. While a standalone VPS self-update is in progress, the **Super Admin → Update** entry is now decorated with small spinning arrows, so a super admin sees a running update straight from the menu instead of having to open `/superadmin/update`. The indicator follows the same route-based registry pattern as the existing administrator warning triangles: one shared indicator renderer now draws both the warning and the running state, and the running state is resolved server-side only for the super admin, so nobody else learns about VPS operations. Whether a self-update is really in progress is decided by one shared `isVpsSelfUpdateJobRunning` check, which the update launcher and the installed-version cleanup use as well, so a job whose installer process died without writing its final status is not reported as running.\n\n-   **Breaking:** Removed the `COMPONENT`, `WALLET` / `WALLETS`, `MEMORY` / `MEMORIES`, `USE BROWSER`, `USE DEEPSEARCH`, `USE SEARCH ENGINE`, `USE SPAWN`, `USE TIMEOUT`, `USE TIME`, `USE EMAIL` and generic `META` commitments from the Book language without any backwards compatibility. `COMPONENT` describes the UI that runs the agent, and wallet, memory, browsing, deep search, web search, timeouts, current time, and e-mail are capabilities of the Agent Server which every agent gets anyway, so none of them belongs in the agent source; `USE SPAWN` was unused. The commitment folders, their tool definitions, tool functions, runtime adapters and system-message aggregation were deleted, together with the `USE` system-message aggregation step, the browser / search / e-mail / timeout / memory / wallet **agent capabilities** shown on agent profiles, the matching entries of the New agent wizard (including its e-mail setup step and translations), and the `USE EMAIL` extraction which the Agent Server used to derive per-agent e-mail configuration from the agent source — e-mail sending is now resolved for every agent from the [user wallet](apps/agents-server/src/utils/useEmailSmtpWalletConstants.ts) alone. The generic `META <TYPE> <content>` catch-all is gone as well: only concrete `META` commitments are commitments now, so `META TITLE`, `META AUTHOR` or any other free-form `META` line is no longer parsed. Because of that, `META DESCRIPTION` (whose definition already existed but was never registered), `META FULLNAME` and the low-level `META ID` are now first-class commitments with their own definitions, which keeps agent descriptions, display names, and permanent ids working exactly as before. `fetchUrlContent` moved from the `USE BROWSER` commitment to [`src/scrapers/_common/utils/fetchUrlContent.ts`](src/scrapers/_common/utils/fetchUrlContent.ts) because it is a scraping utility used by the Agent Server `run_browser` tool and the `/api/scrape` route, and the Agent Server keeps all of its own runtime features — the browser tool, `send_email`, `spawn_agent`, user memory, user wallet, and chat timeouts — since they are server functionality rather than agent source syntax. The Book language documentation, the standalone Book language markdown, the commitment dictionary, the specs, the READMEs, the VSCode grammar, and the bundled default agent books were updated accordingly.\n\n-   Added the `N*M` notation to `--count` of `ptbk coder generate-boilerplates`, which now controls not only how many prompt files are generated but also how many prompts are written into each of them. `--count 10*7` creates 10 files with 7 prompts each, while a plain `--count 10` keeps the previous meaning and is treated as `--count 10*1`. The default is `5*1`, so one generated file contains exactly one prompt instead of the four identical copies it used to contain, and the `coder:generate-boilerplates` script which `ptbk coder init` writes into `package.json` uses `--count 5*1` as well. More than one prompt per file is an advanced option: every single generated prompt is one separate coding task, so each of them is separated by a `---` line and reserves **its own fresh emoji tag** instead of sharing one tag with the rest of the file. A `--count` value which is not one or two positive integers is now refused with an actionable error instead of silently falling back to 5 files, the `--count` parsing is shared by the CLI command and the `generate-prompt-boilerplate` repository script, and the `ptbk coder` landing page lists the new notation among the advanced features.\n\n-   Added `ptbk coder ping`, which sends one tiny dummy prompt through a selected harness and model — for example `ptbk coder ping --harness openai-codex --model gpt-5.6-sol --thinking-level xhigh` — and reports the answer of the harness, the measured response time and the usage the harness reported for it. The ping is built on the very same runner the coding queue uses, so it really exercises the configured harness, model, thinking level and authentication (including the rate-limit retry behavior) instead of only checking that the harness command is installed. Besides testing that a connection works and how fast it answers, it is meant to be run **before** you actually need the harness: the tiny prompt starts the hourly/weekly quota window, so the refresh clock is already running by the time the real coding starts. The dummy work needs no tool and explicitly forbids reading, writing or changing anything, and both temporary artifacts the ping creates are removed again, so the project is left exactly as it was — nothing is written, changed or committed. `--no-ui` streams the raw harness output instead of the compact result, and `--allow-credits` behaves as in `ptbk coder run`. The `ptbk coder` landing page documents the new command among the advanced features.\n\n-   Added `--commit`, `--auto-push` and `--auto-pull` to `ptbk coder init`, `ptbk coder add`, `ptbk coder generate-boilerplates` and `ptbk coder verify`. These commands change project files but used to leave the result uncommitted; now `--auto-pull` pulls the latest changes before the command changes anything, `--commit` commits what the command created with the coding-agent git identity, and `--auto-push` pushes that commit to the remote repository. `ptbk coder verify` applies the synchronization around each single verification, so archiving a finished prompt file and appending a repair prompt are committed and pushed one by one instead of at the end of the whole session. All four commands share one implementation of the pulling, committing and pushing, a repository without any change is never committed as an empty commit, and `--auto-push` without `--commit` is refused with an actionable error. `ptbk coder run` and `ptbk coder server`, which already commit every successful round by default, are unchanged. As part of this, the temporary commit message file which `ptbk coder` writes inside the project is now always kept out of the created commit, so a project which does not keep the Promptbook temporary directory out of version control is no longer left with a dirty working tree after committing.\n\n-   Optimized the startup time of the `ptbk` CLI utility. Simply running `ptbk about` used to take several seconds because the published bundle eagerly loaded the heavy third-party dependencies of the whole engine — `jsdom`, `@mozilla/readability`, `@openai/agents`, `openai`, `@anthropic-ai/sdk`, `@azure/openai`, `jszip`, `socket.io-client` and `prompts` — even for commands that never touch them. These packages are now imported on first use through one shared `createLazyModuleLoader` utility, so a command pays for a dependency only when it really uses it; the repository scripts load `typescript` and `pg` the same way. Every command, option and output stays exactly the same; the website scraper, the OpenAI AgentKit tools, the LLM providers, the `.bookc` archive reader/writer, the remote client and the interactive prompts just load their SDK at the moment they need it. Measured on the generated `@promptbook/cli` bundle, `ptbk about` dropped from about 4.6 s to about 1.8 s, which is roughly 2.8 s saved on every single `ptbk` invocation.\n\n-   Optimized standalone Agents Server self-updates. The request-aware root layout now declares its dynamic boundary before static prerendering can start database-backed work, CLI-owned release builds no longer write unusable multi-gigabyte webpack filesystem caches, retained release caches are reclaimed before deployment, and each update phase records its elapsed time in the installer log.\n\n-   Fixed Agents Server ElevenLabs text-to-speech configuration to use only `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY`; support for the legacy `ELEVEN_LABS_API_KEY` environment variable was removed.\n\n-   Added `--test-before <no|yes-and-fail|yes-and-fix>` to `ptbk coder run`. Pre-coding verification is disabled by default, can stop the run with the complete test output when existing tests fail, or can create and run one shared-format repair prompt before the normal coding queue; an explicit `--test` command is used when provided and `npm test` is the default for the enabled modes. The Coder landing page and local VS Code coder terminals now document and use the repair mode.\n\n-   Fixed preventive generated-project DNS guidance in Agents Server **Super Admin → Servers**. Every registered server now shows the preferred wildcard CNAME record for all current and future project hostnames before its first project is assigned, while assigned project domains remain listed with the shared setup guidance.\n-   Fixed the self-contained Agents Server Stalwart mail service health check so it verifies the public `mail.<domain>` hostname resolves to the VPS, rather than reporting only local API, bridge, and inbound-hook configuration as operational. `/admin/email-server` now flags stale/misconfigured inbound-mail DNS with the detected addresses and fills its copyable A records from the installer’s known VPS public address. The installer now asks for the canonical `mail.<domain>` A record and domain MX record together with the web A record, preventing a fresh VPS from being installed with an unreachable inbound mail target.\n\n-   Added a configurable secure-password generator to the Agents Server `/admin/users` create-user flow. The generator now opens in its own dialog, starts with a secure 16-character configuration (uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and special characters), lets administrators adjust the length and included character categories, and returns the selected generated password to the create-user form. It reuses browser Web Crypto with unbiased sampling, guarantees every selected category is represented, and never permits an empty character set.\n\n-   Fixed Agents Server live chat progress for the default OpenAI Codex local runner. The runner now opts into Codex JSONL events only for Agents Server chats, so the existing progress-card sync can replace the rotating `THINKING_MESSAGES` placeholder as soon as Codex starts a real action. The shared runtime-log resolver turns those events into brief, safe lines such as **\"Inspecting relevant files.\"**, **\"Running tests.\"**, and **\"Updated relevant files.\"**; it deliberately never exposes command text, tool payloads, or private reasoning. Other `ptbk agent-folder` and Codex runs keep their existing human-readable output.\n\n-   Added an Agents Server internal S3 file browser to `/admin/internal-s3`, with folder-style listings under the configured prefix, breadcrumbs, parent navigation, object metadata, and direct file links. Superadmins can switch between the VPS-wide Internal S3 view and the current server's `/admin/files` gallery through shared Storage tabs, while normal admins retain access only to their server's files. The files gallery now uses SQLite-compatible file and agent queries, preventing blank cells, missing dates, and `NaN KB` file sizes.\n\n-   Added `--isolate` to `ptbk coder run`, which keeps the working tree you started the coder from untouched while a task is being implemented. Every prompt gets its own temporary git worktree in `.promptbook/coder-isolation-worktrees/<task-name>` on branch `ptbk-coder-isolation/<task-name>`, with its own copy of the project `.env`, and the coding agent, the `--test` verification command and the round commit all happen inside it. As soon as the task is implemented and verified, it is merged back into the branch the coder runs on as one commit — exactly like a non-isolated round — and the worktree together with its branch is deleted. When the merge fails, the task is marked as `[!]` instead of `[x]`, a commit describing the failed merge and the manual recovery steps is written into the original worktree, the temporary worktree is kept so the changes can be merged by hand, and the coder simply continues with the next task instead of stopping.\n\n    -   `--isolate` now works on Windows. An isolated worktree nests the whole repository below `.promptbook/coder-isolation-worktrees/<task-name>`, so repository paths which still fit into the Windows `MAX_PATH` limit inside the project no longer fit inside the worktree. Git long path support is therefore enabled for every process an isolated run starts, which fixes `error: unable to create file …: Filename too long` followed by `fatal: Could not reset index file to revision 'HEAD'` while creating the worktree. It also fixes the far quieter consequence of the same limit: without it, git reported every too-long path inside the worktree as deleted, so the round commit would have merged mass file deletions back into your branch.\n    -   A worktree which still cannot be checked out is now removed again instead of being left half-written, and the failure is reported as one branded error which names the git lines that explain it, instead of thousands of `Updating files: <percentage>` progress lines.\n\n-   Improved the Agents Server **Book language manual**. A manual exported in Czech is now really written in Czech: all manual prose, chapter titles, catalog labels, examples and pitfalls come from language packs resolved by the requested export language (commitment reference bodies stay in their canonical English, because they are the specification of the keywords). The **Execution and compilation model** chapter was removed, deprecated commitments (such as `TEMPLATE`) are no longer documented at all, and low-level commitments (such as `MODEL`) moved into a closing **Low level commitments** chapter that is opt-in through a new, by default unchecked, download option. The PDF export is now branded with the Promptbook logo, claim, accent color and export metadata, renders every `book` code block with the same syntax colors as `<BookEditor/>`, and wraps pages far better: commitment documentation headings are nested under their catalog entry instead of jumping back to chapter level, headings stay with their content, and long code blocks may split instead of pushing a third of a page of whitespace.\n\n-   Upgraded the **Cloudflare setup wizard** in every Agents Server DNS record manual from step-by-step retyping to two batch imports, so an administrator no longer configures the records of `/superadmin/servers` and `/admin/email-server` one at a time. **Import with API token** writes every shown record into the matching Cloudflare zone with one click using a pasted `Zone.DNS` token (or the `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` already configured on the VPS) and reports per record whether it was created, updated, already configured, skipped, or rejected. **Import zone file** generates a downloadable BIND zone file for Cloudflare's **Import and Export** screen without any credentials. Both ways share one batch plan, so placeholder values such as `<VPS_PUBLIC_IP>` and record alternatives are never written automatically and are listed with the reason instead; existing conflicting Cloudflare records are never deleted, and only records which can hold a single value per hostname (`A`, `AAAA`, `CNAME`, and matching policy `TXT` records) are overwritten. The manual steps and the propagation check remain available as a fallback. The Cloudflare API client is now shared between the Agents Server and the `sync-vercel-domains` script instead of existing twice, and it translates `MX` priorities and `CAA` values into the structured fields the Cloudflare API expects.\n\n-   Fixed the self-contained **Stalwart Mail Server**, which never received a single management call. The VPS installer bootstrap, the administrator provisioning, the domain/alias/MTA-hook synchronization, and the `/admin/email-server` health snapshot all addressed `http://127.0.0.1:8080/api`, a path Stalwart does not serve, so every call answered HTTP `404`; Stalwart therefore stayed in bootstrap mode without any SMTP listener and no agent could send or receive mail. All management calls now use the JMAP management endpoint that Stalwart publishes as `apiUrl` in `/jmap/session` (`http://127.0.0.1:8080/jmap/`). The installer defines that endpoint once and reuses it for the bootstrap request, the administrator provisioning, and the `PTBK_STALWART_API_URL` value, while Agents Server upgrades an already-persisted legacy `/api` path (or a bare Stalwart base URL) so existing installations recover without a manual `.env` edit. The inbound MTA hook is now also registered with the millisecond response timeout Stalwart expects instead of a `30s` string. **Synchronize Stalwart** on `/admin/email-server` and **Synchronize all domains** on `/superadmin/email-server` now share one button component that reports an unreachable or still-bootstrapping mail service next to the button instead of replacing the page with a Server Components error.\n\n-   Added automatic harness installation checks to `ptbk coder`. Before `ptbk coder run` and `ptbk coder server` start, and at the end of `ptbk coder init`, Promptbook now detects whether the used harness command is installed globally and compares its version with the newest one published to npm; when a harness is missing or outdated it offers to run `npm install -g <package>@latest`. One shared harness registry describes the command and npm package of all supported harnesses (OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cline, Claude Code, Opencode, Gemini CLI), `ptbk coder init` checks OpenAI Codex and Claude Code, and non-interactive terminals only print the manual installation command.\n\n-   Added standardized expandable project chips to Agents Server chat. Agent `[[project]]` references now show their running state and open a compact menu with **Open the project in a new tab** and **Open the project page in a new tab** actions; profile-preview, private-mode, and durable chats reuse one runtime-enriched project reference model and shared markdown-chip renderer. **Every** way an agent mentions its project renders as that same chip now, not only the `[[project]]` token: a link into the project page or into an internal project file such as `/agents/yznzwhgnqpinl1/projects/prague-murders-map/files/index.html`, and the public project URL such as `https://prague-murders-map.live.ptbk.io/` written as a link or as a bare URL, are all replaced by the chip, so the chat shows the **project name** (`Prague Murders Map`) together with its running state instead of a raw URL, and the internal file path is never linked — opening the project from the chip always uses its public URL. A project name without a README heading is humanized for the chip label, so `prague-murders-map` reads as `Prague Murders Map`. One reference model carries the URL prefixes which identify a project, and the shared markdown renderer matches them case-insensitively against link targets and bare URLs, ignoring encoding and trailing slashes, while images, code and links to other projects stay untouched. Because the public project URL is now resolved from the persisted project-domain assignment instead of only from a live runtime, a stopped project is recognized and named as well — its **Open the project in a new tab** action stays disabled until the project runs.\n\n-   Improved Agents Server Book language manuals: downloads now create a standalone PDF or Markdown manual from the selected server agents, use those agents' real Book sources as examples, and put their actually used commitments first. The Documentation toolbar now has one **Download manual** action with format, language, and included-agent options; clearing every agent produces the portable generic manual.\n\n-   Unified Agents Server administrator warning indicators in the **System** menu. A single route-based warning registry now drives the top-level **System** triangle, affected category labels, and individual menu entries, keeping them in sync. In addition to existing resource-monitor, core-agent, Shibboleth, and Agent Projects DNS states, the menu now flags registered-server DNS problems, VPS and per-server email health, and active self-contained S3 failures. Warning details remain gated to the matching administrator or super-admin capability, so regular and anonymous users receive none of these operational states.\n\n-   Fixed Super Admin server renames so saving a name on `/superadmin/servers` also updates that server's `SERVER_NAME` metadata. The metadata write now runs in the explicitly selected server context rather than the administrator's current-server context, preserving isolation across a multi-server VPS; it updates existing SQLite metadata rows reliably and clears stale metadata caches.\n\n-   Added a guided **Cloudflare setup wizard** to every Agents Server DNS record manual. The shared panel now walks administrators through opening the correct Cloudflare zone, adding the existing record-table values with the provider’s field names, using **DNS only** for directly verified A/AAAA/CNAME records, and checking propagation; the record table remains the single source of truth for both server and email DNS instructions.\n\n-   Added the selected `--thinking-level` to successful `ptbk coder` prompt status lines, alongside the harness and model (for example, `by Claude Code \\`claude-opus-4-8\\` thinking \\`xhigh\\``). The Coder landing page now documents this completion metadata.\n\n-   Fixed standalone VPS project DNS visibility: `/superadmin/servers` now verifies generated project hostnames, defaults its setup guidance to the preferred wildcard CNAME record, and labels each owner with a linked agent chip. DNS problems now also appear on affected project pages and the **Agent Projects** menu item.\n\n-   Simplified Agents Server project runtimes to one automatic Run action: projects with a non-empty `package.json` `dev` script now run `npm run dev`, while all other projects use the static server. Admins can now run and stop projects directly from `/admin/projects`.\n\n-   Enhanced the Agents Server `/superadmin/environment` editor so super admins can add arbitrary valid `.env` variables directly from the UI. Every variable already persisted in the VPS `.env` file is now listed automatically — including integrations such as `ELEVEN_LABS_API_KEY` — while sensitive values remain masked and the server-side super-admin-only write policy remains enforced.\n\n-   Fixed the Agents Server home page so the temporary federated-agents loading section is not shown before federation data is available. When no federated servers or agents are returned, the homepage now remains free of that section instead of briefly showing it.\n-   Fixed cross-platform unit-test portability: macOS canonical temporary paths no longer conflict with test assertions or Git exclusions, shell-script links normalize Windows-style separators on every host, document-scraper unit tests no longer require locally installed Pandoc or LibreOffice, import repair handles Windows paths when run on another platform, and Agents Server builds clear stale Next route types left by another build output directory.\n\n-   Fixed the Agents Server home page so the temporary federated-agents loading section is not shown before federation data is available. When no federated servers or agents are returned, the homepage now remains free of that section instead of briefly showing it.\n\n-   Unified Agents Server DNS setup guidance. `/superadmin/servers` and `/admin/email-server` now reuse one record-instruction panel with consistent record columns, setup steps, conflict guidance, and DNS-provider documentation links; server-domain diagnostics still offer one compatible A/AAAA/CNAME alternative, while email setup correctly requires every MX/SPF/DMARC/TLS record shown.\n\n-   Improved Agents Server `/admin/users` with a practical admin table that puts named users first and clearly groups anonymous visitor accounts below them. User creation now opens a create-server-style dialog with a browser Web Crypto secure password generator, and every user links to a detail page with recent chat activity plus direct links to filtered Chat history and Task manager views. Chat history now supports preserving a user filter through table, thread, and CSV views, and task/chat tables link back to the relevant user.\n\n-   Fixed the Agents Server initial chat greeting so a partially loaded agent never shows its opaque permanent id. The canonical chat now reuses the already resolved human-readable agent title until the remote agent profile is available.\n\n-   Fixed the default Coder project npm scripts to use the locally installed `ptbk` command expected by the Coder boilerplate verification.\n\n-   Enhanced Agents Server admin page tabs with one shared underline-style navigation component. Configuration, storage, and task-manager scope tabs now use consistent spacing, active-state styling, hover states, and accessible current-page semantics.\n\n-   Unified the Agents Server per-server and VPS-wide task managers. The VPS-wide `/superadmin/task-manager` now shows the same task details, target links, log controls, task detail links, cancellation/retry actions, terminal button, and bulk cancellation action as `/admin/task-manager`, with only the owning **Server** column added; cross-server actions preserve each server's isolated context, and the former `/admin/task-manager-vps` URL redirects to the new super-admin route.\n\n-   Scoped agent project reporting correctly across standalone VPS servers. The per-server `/admin/projects` dashboard remains limited to agents owned by the current server, while the super-admin `/superadmin/resource-monitor` project storage panel now aggregates every registered server and labels each project with its owning server.
